high.title: Hardcoded encryption key in the app's Dart code
high.description: A Key object is built from the string literal on the cited line, which is compiled into the app. The application uses a hardcoded AES key 'DVFA_STATIC_KEY_8899001122334455' and a hardcoded IV 'DVFA_STATIC_IV__' to encrypt the user's statement, allowing anyone with access to the APK to decrypt sensitive financial data.
high.impact: Anyone who unpacks the app recovers the value and decrypts what it protects.
high.recommendation: Generate keys in the Android Keystore and a fresh random IV for every encryption.

medium.title: Backup-enabled app stores credentials in local storage
medium.description:
3 findings in this app combine into one exploitable path: "Application data is backup-enabled", "Insecure storage of sensitive data in SQLite" and "Sensitive value 'pin' stored in plain SharedPreferences".

Attack path:
1. Attacker triggers adb backup of the app
2. Attacker extracts the backup archive
3. Attacker locates notes_database.db in the backup data
4. Attacker queries the SQLite database
5. Attacker retrieves the Admin Secret from asm/dvfa/notes_screen.dart
medium.impact: Backup copies the app's private storage, and that storage holds a credential. For an app targeting below Android 12 (API 31), or a debuggable one, `adb backup` does it over USB without root, so anyone with a minute at an unlocked phone walks away with the credential; for newer targets it travels in cloud and device-transfer backups.
medium.recommendation: Set android:allowBackup="false", or exclude the credential store via android:dataExtractionRules. Keep tokens in EncryptedSharedPreferences or the Keystore rather than plain SharedPreferences.

medium.title: Input hash compared against a hardcoded hash
medium.description: The app hashes a value - typically an entered PIN or password - and compares the result with a hex digest compiled into the app, so the check is decided on the device against a constant.
medium.impact: The digest ships with the app; a short PIN or password behind it is recovered by hashing every candidate offline, and the comparison is one hook from always passing.
medium.recommendation: Verify credentials on a server, or derive a key from them with a slow KDF.

low.title: SQL statement built by string interpolation and run as a raw query
low.description: An SQL statement literal is joined with runtime values by string interpolation and passed to a raw query call, so a value containing a quote changes the statement. The application performs a raw SQL query using string interpolation of user-supplied search text (line 750), leading to a SQL injection vulnerability in the local notes database. The `_refreshNotes` function constructs a SQL query using string interpolation, concatenating user-controlled input into a `LIKE` clause without sanitization.
low.impact: A local attacker can use SQL injection payloads (e.g., using OR 1=1) to bypass the `is_hidden = 0` filter and retrieve all entries from the notes table, including hidden administrative secrets.
low.recommendation: Pass values as arguments with ? placeholders instead of interpolating them.

info.title: Activity MainActivity receives deep links (dvfa)
info.description: Activity "com.schmiemandev.dvfa.MainActivity" accepts BROWSABLE VIEW links, so any web page, message or QR code can open it with a URL of its choosing. That is its purpose and no permission can guard it; whether it is a vulnerability depends on what its handler does with the link.
info.impact: An entry point every remote attacker can reach with one tap from the victim.
info.recommendation: Treat every value in the link as untrusted, and require the user to confirm before the link changes data or starts a payment.

info.title: Application data is backup-enabled
info.description: android:allowBackup is absent, which defaults to true, so the app's data goes into cloud backups and device-to-device transfers. With targetSdkVersion 36, Android 12 and later leave it out of `adb backup`, so USB extraction needs a device older than Android 12.
info.impact: Locally stored credentials or PII travel with the user's cloud backup and to a new device, and are extractable over USB on devices older than Android 12.
info.recommendation: Set android:allowBackup="false", or exclude sensitive files with android:dataExtractionRules (android:fullBackupContent below Android 12).

reasons: Backup-extractable app data. Backup is a documented platform feature and on by default. What matters is what would be in the backup: name a credential in app storage and this becomes a real extraction path.
This is a platform default that only becomes a vulnerability when paired with sensitive data in storage, as seen in Insecure storage of sensitive data in SQLite.
Confirmed as part of chain-001: Backup-enabled app stores credentials in local storage.

info.title: No network security config declared
info.description: The app declares neither android:networkSecurityConfig nor usesCleartextTraffic, so it relies on platform defaults and pins no domain. With targetSdkVersion 36 those defaults block cleartext HTTP and trust only system CAs.
info.impact: Without pinning, anyone who gets a CA trusted on the device can read and alter the app's TLS traffic.
info.recommendation: Declare a network security config that disables cleartext and pins the domains that carry sensitive traffic.

reasons: No certificate pinning. Pinning defends against an attacker who already controls a trusted CA or the device's trust store. Without one of those, TLS is still doing its job. It becomes a finding when paired with what the unpinned channel actually carries.
Lack of pinning is a configuration state that only provides gain if the attacker can already compromise a CA or the device trust store.

info.description: Nothing in the app sets WindowManager.LayoutParams.FLAG_SECURE, so every screen can be screenshotted or recorded and appears in the recent-apps snapshot.
info.impact: Credentials, balances or personal data on screen end up in screenshots, screen recordings and the task-switcher preview.

reasons: Screen contents not protected from capture. Without FLAG_SECURE, what a screen shows can end up in screenshots, screen recordings and the task-switcher preview. That matters on screens showing credentials, card numbers or balances; on its own it is a hardening note.

info.title: Task hijacking (StrandHogg) possible on Android 10 and lower
info.description: minSdkVersion 24 lets the app run on Android versions before 11, and its task affinity is its package name "com.schmiemandev.dvfa". There, another app can declare the same affinity, with allowTaskReparenting, and have its own activity shown in this app's task.
info.impact: On a device running Android 10 or lower, a malicious app can put a look-alike screen on top of this app's task, phishing credentials or keeping the real app from being shown.
info.recommendation: Raise minSdkVersion to 30, where Android fixed this. Until then, android:taskAffinity="" on the <application> mitigates the original attack, though not its runtime variant on unpatched Android 9 and lower.
